question: Which statement best describes The 'use client' directive?
options: You reach for a Client Component when a piece of UI needs `useState`/`useReducer`, lifecycle/`useEffect`, event handlers like `onClick`/`onChange`, refs to DOM nodes, or React Context that uses those. If a component just renders data, it should stay a Server Component.

Anything that touches `window`, `document`, `localStorage`, `navigator`, geolocation, media, or other browser-only globals must run in a Client Component (typically inside `useEffect`, since those globals don't exist during server render). Accessing them on the server throws.

A Client Component can't IMPORT a Server Component, but it CAN render a Server Component passed to it as `children` or props. So you wrap interactive client chrome around server-rendered content — keeping the heavy/data parts on the server while the wrapper handles interactivity.

Putting `'use client'` as the very first line of a file marks that module — and everything it imports — as a Client Component that ships to the browser. It's the explicit opt-in OUT of the server-default world and into a component that has a client runtime.
explanation: Putting `'use client'` as the very first line of a file marks that module — and everything it imports — as a Client Component that ships to the browser. It's the explicit opt-in OUT of the server-default world and into a component that has a client runtime.

question: Which statement best describes When you actually need it: interactivity?
options: A Client Component can't IMPORT a Server Component, but it CAN render a Server Component passed to it as `children` or props. So you wrap interactive client chrome around server-rendered content — keeping the heavy/data parts on the server while the wrapper handles interactivity.

Everything a `'use client'` file imports is bundled for the browser, so a boundary placed too high drags loads of code (and Server Component logic) into the client. Push `'use client'` to the leaves: make the smallest possible island interactive and leave the rest server-rendered.

question: Which statement best describes Browser APIs?
options: Everything a `'use client'` file imports is bundled for the browser, so a boundary placed too high drags loads of code (and Server Component logic) into the client. Push `'use client'` to the leaves: make the smallest possible island interactive and leave the rest server-rendered.

The server sends HTML for the Client Component (so the user sees content fast), then the browser downloads its JS and HYDRATES it — attaching state and event listeners to the existing DOM. The first render in the browser must match the server HTML, or you get a hydration mismatch warning.
